name: Facial feminization surgery

lead: Facial feminization surgery is a group of operations that soften masculine facial features: lowering the hairline, reshaping the brow ridge, nose and lips, building up the cheeks, and reducing the chin, jaw and Adam's apple. The aim is a more harmonious face with softer features.

It was developed from the early 1980s by Douglas Ousterhout for transgender women. Systematic reviews report improved quality of life and a low complication rate, though the evidence is mostly case series. On looksmax.org some users discuss borrowing its brow, nose and cheek techniques for male faces; that use has not been studied.

paras: Surgeons plan from CT and MRI imaging, then reshape bone, move soft tissue and add cheek volume with implants or fat. The work may be staged or combined into one long operation, with recovery measured in weeks.

Reported risks include nerve injury, infection, implant displacement, fat resorption, bone-healing problems after forehead work, and voice changes after Adam's apple reduction. These are major operations under general anaesthesia; costs can be high and coverage depends on country and insurer.

chain: Brow, nose, cheek and jaw reshaped
angle.text: The payoff is a face with softer, more harmonious features, with the brow, nose, cheeks and jaw reshaped. Surgeons work on bone and soft tissue, so changes are visible after healing. Developed for transgender women, it is also discussed in forums for male faces.

lead: Facial feminization surgery (FFS) is an umbrella term for reconstructive procedures that alter typically masculine facial features toward more typically feminine ones. It is performed mostly for transgender women and other transfeminine people, and includes work on the hairline, forehead and brow ridge, nose, cheeks, lips, chin and jaw, and the thyroid cartilage (Adam's apple) [1][2].

Its techniques derive from maxillofacial, ear-nose-throat and plastic and reconstructive surgery. Surgeon Douglas Ousterhout is credited with pioneering most of the procedures beginning in the early 1980s [1][2]. Systematic reviews describe improved well-being and quality of life after FFS with a low complication rate, while noting that the evidence base is mostly case series [1][2].

In looksmaxxing communities, FFS is discussed in a different framing: some users on looksmax.org consider borrowing its brow, nose and cheek techniques to alter forehead, eye area and facial width in men [3].
infobox: Gender dysphoria related to facial appearance
Hairline, brow bone, rhinoplasty, cheek, lip, chin and jaw, tracheal shave

paras: Surgeons commonly use CT and MRI imaging to identify features and plan the operation [1]. Procedures are grouped by thirds of the face.

Upper third: the hairline may be lowered, advanced or restored with transplant grafts. The brow ridge can be sanded down, or where the frontal sinus lies behind it, the bone can be reshaped and refixed (cranioplasty). A brow lift can reposition the eyebrows above the ridge, and orbital reconstruction can change eye socket shape [1]. Wikipedia notes that data do not clearly favour one method of ridge reduction over the other and that results data on orbital work are limited [1].

Middle third: rhinoplasty reduces nose size and reshapes the tip, cheeks may be built up with implants or fat grafts, and a lip lift shortens the upper lip [1]. Lower third: chin length can be reduced by shaving or sliding genioplasty, the jaw angle and masseter muscle can be reduced, and a chondrolaryngoplasty (tracheal shave) reduces the Adam's apple [1]. A Grokipedia summary lists the same family of procedures and describes typical costs in the United States of roughly 35,000 to 70,000 dollars or more for extensive work [2].

Wikipedia lists risks by procedure: nerve injury (mental nerve damage being the main concern in chin and jaw work), tooth root injury, infection, bone non-union, implant displacement, resorption of grafted fat, impaired nasal valve function, cysts and bone-healing problems after forehead work, and vocal cord injury after tracheal shave. It describes overall complication rates as low and notes many can be corrected with further surgery [1]. Grokipedia, which is AI-generated, reports complication rates of 5 to 25 percent across studies and attributes this to heterogeneous low-evidence reporting [2].

In 1982, Darrell Pratt, a surgeon performing genital reassignment surgery, asked Douglas Ousterhout to operate on a transgender woman whose face still drew male-gendered reactions. Ousterhout, who had reconstructed faces affected by birth defects and trauma, studied early twentieth-century anthropology and cephalometric measurements to define femininity, and tested his measurements on hundreds of skulls [1]. His 2009 book on the topic is cited as a foundation of the field [1].

Coverage varies. Wikipedia reports that insurers commonly cover FFS in France, Belgium and the Netherlands, that coverage is difficult to obtain in Germany, and that in the United States coverage has increased since the Affordable Care Act, with state laws barring exclusion of gender-affirming care [1]. A psychotherapeutic letter is generally required in clinical practice [1].

Grokipedia presents a more critical framing, raising questions about causal effects on dysphoria, noting that research on social perception has rated some post-FFS faces as less attractive and more masculine than cisgender female faces, and citing reports of regret [2]. These claims are attributed to that AI-generated source and were not independently checked against the primary studies.

A 2016 systematic review by Morrison and colleagues concluded that FFS can significantly improve well-being and quality of life by reducing gender dysphoria, with a low complication rate [1]. A 2017 review by Berli and colleagues said the evidence had reached a higher level and recommended that FFS procedures be included in international guidelines as medically necessary [1]. A 2010 study by Ainsworth and Spiegel found mental-health-related quality of life statistically lower in transgender women with no surgery than in the general female population, and than in those who had genital surgery, FFS or both [1]. Spiegel (2011) concluded that the forehead and upper third had greater influence on gender perception than the lower jaw or midface [1]. Grokipedia reports short-term satisfaction above 80 percent in systematic reviews and notes limited long-term data [2].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, FFS appears as a source of techniques for men who feel their faces look 'ogre' or heavy-browed; participants discuss it alongside implants and other hardmaxx options [3].

claims.claim: FFS techniques such as brow bone shaping and cheek augmentation can remove 'ogre' features and improve harmony in a male face.
Combining FFS with implants would cost more than just getting cheek implants and some brow and nose reshaping.

timeline.event: Douglas Ousterhout operates on a transgender woman at the request of surgeon Darrell Pratt, beginning the development of FFS [1].
Ousterhout publishes a guide to FFS for transgender women [1].
Morrison and colleagues publish a systematic review of FFS outcomes [1].
Berli and colleagues review the evidence and recommend inclusion in guidelines [1].
